title: ‘The Invisible Guest’ Remake Director Danial Rifki on Suharto-Era Fear and Why His New Thriller Is About ‘How to Fight Back’
description: Indonesian director Danial Rifki’s remake of Spanish thriller “The Invisible Guest,” which he says was completed in 2023 before exclusivity clauses
body:
Indonesian director Danial Rifki’s remake of Spanish thriller “The Invisible Guest,” which he says was completed in 2023 before exclusivity clauses with HBO held up its release, finally reached the big screen at Jakarta World Cinema. 

	It is one of three Rifki films at the festival.

	The Falcon Pictures production, which reworks Oriol Paulo’s 2016 hit “Contratiempo” for an Indonesian setting, stars Reza Rahadian, Mawar de Jongh and Arifin Putra. It debuted on HBO Max on Aug. 7.
	

	Rifki tells Variety that the matter has only recently been resolved.

	He also has two new features at the festival: romantic comedy “Tua Tua Keladi” and thriller “Sandal Jepit No. 10.”

	Set among the older residents of a small village, “Tua Tua Keladi” follows the chaos that breaks out when a chemical leak into the village water supply stirs up desire. Unspoken feelings, long-held confessions and passion come out overnight.

	“I was thinking, if they have young energy to live the second life, [it is] the second chance to love,” Rifki says.

	He wanted the film to challenge a deep-rooted assumption that older people no longer live with energy. For all the awkwardness of its premise, the film keeps away from eroticism, even with its younger characters.

	In the digital era, Rifki says, people can record their sexual behavior openly – “and sometimes that kind of freaks me out because I have a daughter. I’m concerned if my daughter [is exposed to] wild media.”

	“So with the young characters, I try to approach them with something pure, not physical,” he says.
	

	“Sandal Jepit No. 10” is a confined-space thriller about the brutal police interrogation of Akbar, a grieving father detained on suspicion of murder.

	“Indonesians have trauma in politics. Life back in the days of Orde Baru – the New Order in the Suharto era – for around 32 years, we could not criticize the government,” Rifki says. “Now we have the Reformation Era, but it might be happening underground. On social media, if you criticize the government, they will shadowban [your comment].”

	“We are the low class of society with this kind of fear that, if we do something, someone with power will oppress us. So the movie is about how to fight back,” he says.

	“If you have social media, netizens are here to help you out. People power now is turning [to] a digital era so we can gain that power again. I’m still sure that [there are] many good people,” he adds.

	Rifki says the film grew out of his concern over abuse of power in Indonesia today.

	“[When I was] a film student, I really wanted to try how to speak in rom-com, thriller, drama, and other genres. [I’m] an evolving and growing filmmaker still in the making,” he says.

	The backbone of all his work, he says, is human moral conflict, whatever the genre. He is also keen to try action and horror.

	His next film, “Before Thirty,” is set for release in January 2027. Rifki calls it a “survival drama” about a 29-year-old man whose life is failing.

	“In Indonesia, people always ask: what is your achievement before 30? Young people are punished by that value that you have to be successful before the age of 30,” Rifki says.

	The film, he says, is his “commentary on that issue.”

schema.headline: ‘The Invisible Guest’ Remake Director Danial Rifki on Suharto-Era Fear and Why His New Thriller Is About ‘How to Fight Back’

title: Sylvester Stallone Says His 20-Year Rivalry With Arnold Schwarzenegger Only Ended When He Ran for Governor and Wasn’t ‘Doing Movies Anymore’
description: Sylvester Stallone is reminiscing about his now-infamous rivalry with fellow action star Arnold Schwarzenegger through the 1980s and 1990s — and wh
body:
Sylvester Stallone is reminiscing about his now-infamous rivalry with fellow action star Arnold Schwarzenegger through the 1980s and 1990s — and why they only laid down the hatchet when the latter ran for governor of California.

	In a recent interview on “The Rest Is Entertainment” podcast, the “Rocky” actor answered whether he felt the competition between the two actors shaped his career and led him to take risks.


	“Yeah, it did,” said Stallone. “You know, we were very confrontational.” He continued: “Because you have two people arriving at the beginning of a different genre and we both want to be in charge of that genre. I never wanted to be an action guy, but I did ‘First Blood’ and I said, ‘This is interesting because action films, if done right, are modern mythology. It’s like what they used to do, you know, ‘The Iliad’ and ‘The Odyssey’ and Hercules and Achilles.’”
	

	“So, I see this guy, and I could tell right away he’s going to be a problem,” Stallone said, referring to Schwarzenegger. “You know, we were at the Golden Globe Awards, and he’s sitting there and he’s eyeballing me, and — we call that stink eye — I said, ‘Okay, all right. I got it, pal.’ And then he wins.”

	The two continued to vie for the title of top action star, with both actors liking “to challenge” one another, said Stallone. “We’re both physical, and now, who’s going to be the vanguard, the leader in that genre? So I do ‘Rambo,’ he does ‘Commando,’ and it went back and forth, back and forth, on and off screen. It was very contentious, trust me. Which I enjoyed.” The two later partnered on the movie-themed chain restaurant Planet Hollywood in 1991, but Stallone noted that they wouldn’t even get on stage together to give a speech.
	

	Their rivalry “wasn’t put to bed until 20 years later,” said Stallone, when Schwarzenegger decided to run for governor. “We went to the same cigar place. He was there. I said, ‘Enough of this. We’re not in competition anymore.’ He’s not doing movies anymore. All right. Thank you very much for waking me up and lighting a fire under me. And he felt the same way.”

	To this day, they remain friendly — “We’re always going to be competitive… That’s the nature of the beast, and I enjoy it. I really do. But we’re not as financially competitive anymore,” Stallone concluded.

schema.headline: Sylvester Stallone Says His 20-Year Rivalry With Arnold Schwarzenegger Only Ended When He Ran for Governor and Wasn’t ‘Doing Movies Anymore’

title: IP Companies Spin Books Into Sold-Out Plays, Series and Signature Scents at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
description: Taiwanese companies laid out how original stories can grow from books into stage plays, series, fragrances and even travel itineraries at a Taiwan
body:
Taiwanese companies laid out how original stories can grow from books into stage plays, series, fragrances and even travel itineraries at a Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) session on cross-sector intellectual property in Taipei.

	“The original intention behind developing IP is for the industry to thrive together, so everyone can make money,” said Mimi Wang, COO of Taiwanese IP development company IPis Innovation.


	Wang said the approach was partly modeled on South Korea, where IP adaptation began 30 years ago. “Policies brought in industries such as fashion and electronics to collaborate and invest in developing cultural products. That was also the origin of the Korean Wave,” she said.
	

	IPis often starts with books, which Wang said offer a cheaper way to find stories that already have readers. A stage production can then test audience demand through ticket sales before the company moves into screen adaptations and related products.

	The company’s stage play “Marital Lost Love” is based on a book by psychiatrist Deng Hui-wen. After three runs that Wang said sold out, IPis extended the project with a podcast and two fragrances tied to the production.

	Its series project “Do You Still Love Me?” was developed from a novel written as the story source. The project won five awards at TCCF Pitching in 2025, more than any other project that year, including the udnFunLife IP Potential Award. Wang said the pitch worked because it told a clear, engaging story and showed how it could reach audiences and open up business opportunities.

	Wang said plans for the project include brand partnerships and product placement, a revival of the reality show “Love Battle” and a related feature film, “99 Days to Countdown.” The film’s honeymoon trip could also become a travel itinerary built with tourism partners.
	

	“Our IP development plan has three main pillars: emotional resonance, ESG [environmental, social and governance] and Taiwanese values,” Wang said.

	For Taiwanese identity, she pointed to “Siwei Street No. 1,” by Yang Shuang-zi, the author of National Book Award winner “Taiwan Travelogue.” The novel follows five women sharing a house in Taichung. IPis plans a stage version alongside food events drawing on a Japanese colonial-era Taiwanese cookbook featured in the story.

	Other ideas include a Taiwanese banquet, an exhibition, scent-based products and character booklets. Wang said Japanese partners had already shown interest in licensing or other forms of collaboration.

	“A successful investment needs three key conditions: profitability, stability and growth,” said Erica Wang, CEO of the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), which organizes TCCF. “In the IP field, we need to find that formula for profitability through a ‘one source, multiple uses’ approach.”

	Owen Lee, chair of udnFunLife, the events and ticketing arm of Taiwan’s United Daily News Group, said his company focuses on cross-industry uses of IP, including theater, exhibitions, experiences and merchandise, while leaving the original creative work to creators. It invests in projects and helps work out how to bring them to audiences and sell them, he said.

	For investors, Lee said, extending an IP depends partly on whether the rights are available. His company seeks priority rights to develop extensions and checks whether adaptation and sequel rights are clear, and whether permissions for performers, characters and music would need to be renegotiated for each new use.

	Lee also weighs an IP’s “spillover value”: whether audiences recognize it and whether its premise adapts easily to other formats. A clear, accessible title can cut the marketing needed to explain a project to new audiences, he said, while cost and timing also shape which extension fits.

	He cited an exhibition built around Taiwanese horror film “The Rope Curse 3” before its release, using material from the franchise to build interest. A mobile VR experience was being planned around “The Rope Curse 4,” he said.

	Lee said he sees strong potential in Taiwan’s live-action film, TV and theater IP, while character-based properties and animation still have room to grow. For Mimi Wang, the starting point remains the audience: creators, she said, should ask what viewers want to see and how a personal story can speak to a wider public.

schema.headline: IP Companies Spin Books Into Sold-Out Plays, Series and Signature Scents at Taiwan Creative Content Fest

title: Murder-House Impostor Thriller ‘The Stand-In Family’ Wins Mirror Fiction Award at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
description: Taiwanese literary IP developer and production company Mirror Fiction announced the winners of its fifth Mirror Fiction Award and unveiled five pro
body:
Taiwanese literary IP developer and production company Mirror Fiction announced the winners of its fifth Mirror Fiction Award and unveiled five projects for its 2027 slate at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF).

	The NT$1 million ($32,000) Grand Prize went to Iris Kong for “The Stand-In Family” (provisional title), a suspense novel about four strangers who impersonate a family inside a house where a murder has taken place. Under the surveillance of a property developer, one of them is forced to confront a past wrongdoing.
	

	“This award was a clear goal for me when I created the story,” said Kong, an engineer by profession. “I had written other works before, but adapting them for the screen would have been too expensive. So this time, I started with a realistic setting and considered production costs from the beginning.”

	The NT$700,000 ($22,500) Judges’ Award went to Malaysian writer Liang Xuan for “Endless Rain” (provisional title). Both winning works are eligible for publication and screen adaptation development through Mirror Fiction.

	Tung Cheng-yu, CEO of Mirror Fiction, said the award was designed to encourage writers and introduce promising literary properties to potential investors. “I believe that only when you genuinely fall in love with a story can you make the best adaptation,” Tung said. “Adapting a novel for the screen is much easier than starting from scratch because the novel already has an established world,” she said.

	Citing audience figures, Tung said films adapted from books drew more than 40% higher attendance than original films, while the difference for television content exceeded 60%. She did not identify the source of the figures during the presentation.
	

	The fifth edition of the award received 529 submissions totaling more than 40 million Chinese characters, with the winners selected through multiple rounds of judging.

	In the second half of the showcase, Mirror Fiction sales director Sharleen Liu introduced five literary projects on the company’s 2027 IP slate.

	Leading the lineup was “036037,” a contemporary romance novel by Kevin Chen, whose novel “Ghost Town” has been published in English. The story follows two middle-aged people revisiting a relationship from more than two decades earlier, exploring regret and the possibility of moving on. The novel has already secured a screen adaptation deal, with a four-volume print edition scheduled for December.

	“The Midnight Masseuse: A Taipei Noir,” by Tommy Tan, begins with the murder of a female massage therapist and unfolds into a crime thriller exposing connections among police officers, prosecutors, politicians and business interests.

	“Double Diplomacy,” by Daniel Hsieh, follows two brothers, one a diplomat and the other a criminal strategist, who exchange identities. Their encounters with each other’s worlds draw them into a diplomatic crisis involving international negotiations and organized crime.

	“Red-Haired Inibs,” by Indigenous writer and historian Nakao Eki Pacidal, follows a girl of mixed Indigenous and Dutch ancestry in 17th-century Taiwan. Inibs were female priests of the Indigenous Siraya people. Her search for her father becomes a journey into identity, belonging and the lives of people left out of official historical accounts.

	The slate is rounded out by Kong’s “The Stand-In Family.”

	Mirror Fiction, which develops literary properties for publication and cross-media adaptation, has also expanded into film and television investment and production. Its credits include the Netflix series “The Victims’ Game,” which won at Taiwan’s Golden Bell Awards, the country’s top TV honors. Its investments include Chung Mong-hong’s “The Falls,” Taiwan’s Oscar submission, and horror film “The Rope Curse 3.”

title: AI Could Make Filmmaking Costlier Than the 35mm Era, Korean Pioneers Warn at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
description: AI is already slashing the cost of commercials, but runaway token fees and piecemeal revisions could leave feature producers paying more than in th
body:
AI is already slashing the cost of commercials, but runaway token fees and piecemeal revisions could leave feature producers paying more than in the days of 35mm film, a Korean AI production pioneer told Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.

	Kim Kwang-jib, founder and CEO of AI content studio Studio Meta-K, said that with the most expensive commercial tools, the token bill alone for a 100-minute film can top KRW500 million ($366,000). AI companies are all losing money, he said, and are keeping prices low as a marketing play.
	

	“If they raise token costs roughly tenfold, it could go above what the films we’re shooting now cost,” Kim said. “KRW500 million could become KRW5 billion ($3.66 million).”

	Hollywood, with KRW200 billion ($146.6 million) budgets, could absorb that and still make very cheap AI films, Kim said. Korean, Taiwanese and other Asian features typically shoot live action and VFX for KRW3 billion-KRW5 billion ($2.2 million-$3.66 million), and a tenfold jump would force them to ask whether AI is efficient at all.

	He drew a line back to celluloid. Preproduction was meticulous when every take burned through film stock, then digital let crews shoot and cut freely without extra cost. With AI, every re-render is paid for again. If a client sends 10 changes at once, Kim said, Studio Meta-K can make them all and re-render a single time, paying for just one extra pass. If the same 10 changes arrive one a day over 10 days, the studio has to re-render 10 times and pay 10 times over. The final budget, he said, comes down to how few rounds of revisions there are.
	

	“Unless the preproduction stage is made solid, I think AI could end up spending even more money than in the 35mm film era,” he said.

	Lee Sang-wook, head of the AI Content Lab at MBC C&I, a subsidiary of Korean broadcaster MBC, said budgeting is harder still because the tools keep moving. His lab’s 139-minute feature “Raphael” took around a year and four months to make, and new tools and updates arrive weekly.

	“If you apply technology from a year ago, the scenes look very old,” Lee said.

	He added that a single shot on “Raphael” sometimes tied up around 10 artists for an entire day. The film was made with emerging directors discovered by the lab, who raised investment and set up their own studio, and the lab’s work drew backing from Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Creative Content Agency. “Raphael” will open in Korean cinemas on Nov. 25.

	The lab began experimenting with generative AI shorts in 2024, before packaging AI content as a genre strand, “The Prompt: Next Drama,” on Korean streamer Wavve.

	“When we made AI short films in 2024, the market reaction was very cold, in Korea as well,” Lee said.

	He wanted to face audiences directly, he said, and a cinema release can move to streaming later while the reverse order is hard. He also wanted to show that AI studios, many of which work on an outsourcing model, can take commercial bets through IP development.

	On commercials, Kim cited a Pizza Hut spot that aired on TV last year, which took about eight months and roughly KRW2 billion ($1.4 million) to produce. A version Studio Meta-K made in-house took about two weeks and around KRW30 million ($22,000), or about 2% of the cost. In advertising, he said, production costs can fall by more than 90%.

	Drama is a harder sell. Kim does not think audiences will yet pay to watch fully AI films or series, so he favors a hybrid model with star actors. A scene requiring more than 500 extras, with costumes, hair and makeup to match, could be generated with AI, leaving only the close-ups of the leads to shoot live. The company is producing war scenes with AI for KBS program “History Special.”

	His larger pitch was to reverse the pipeline. Rather than calling in AI after a shoot and edit have already eaten the budget, Studio Meta-K is testing building an entire 100-minute film at film-like quality in preproduction, then reshooting only the parts that feel off, such as emotional bust shots. For now perhaps 50 of those 100 minutes would need to be reshot in live action, Kim said, but he expects that eventually nothing will need shooting at all.
	

	Kim founded Studio Meta-K in 2022 as a K-drama and film company alongside well-known drama directors and writers. Its stated aim is to use AI to cut production costs and own IP rather than take outsourced work, and it has completed more than 100 commercial projects. This year the company was selected for two government R&D projects worth about KRW15 billion ($11 million) combined to build SaaS-based platforms, leading a consortium that includes an MBC subsidiary, KBS and MBN. Studio Meta-K raised around KRW3 billion ($2.2 million) in a Series A last year and around KRW10 billion ($7.3 million) this month, and is preparing for an IPO next year.

	The company is also turning Im Kwon-taek’s 1993 classic “Seopyeonje” into an animated feature, re-editing the original footage and converting it into animation with AI for a theatrical release next summer. The project, a collaboration with Busan’s Dongseo University, has the director’s involvement. Studio Meta-K has several animated features in production simultaneously.

	The two companies split on open-source tools. Kim said free open-source models have improved sharply, and on one animated project Studio Meta-K builds easy shots with open-source tools and reserves paid commercial tools for difficult ones. Lee said MBC C&I steers away from open-source because it cannot verify the transparency of the training data, noting that no AI model yet meets EU AI Act guidelines. The company has also joined C2PA.

	Lee said delivery to streamers is tougher than meeting cinema DCP specs, since platforms analyze files mechanically rather than by eye, and AI output still struggles with requirements such as bitrate and color grading. Kim expects issues like color depth and bitrate to be solved soon.

	On jobs, Kim said crews of hundreds on a single scene will grow rarer, and roles such as drone operators and set work could largely disappear. Some companies are already keeping preproduction staff and laying off production crews in favor of co-producing with Studio Meta-K, he said.

	“I don’t see AI replacing that workforce,” Kim said. “I personally think workers who have learned AI will replace workers who haven’t.”

	Lee compared the shift to the arrival of sound, which cost theater musicians their jobs, and the move from film to digital cameras, which raised the editor’s importance. He predicted new roles including previsualization artists who break down scripts into previs, and continuity supervisors charged with keeping locations and characters consistent. One studio in Korea already has more than 50 AI artists working together, he said, and technical directors will matter more as the technology advances. Spatial consistency, he added, is harder to achieve than character consistency.
	

	Actors, Lee said, have warmed to AI. On a daily drama, previs of a dangerous accident scene turned cast skepticism into approval once performers saw AI would handle shots that could injure them. He does not believe AI can ultimately replace actors’ emotional detail.

	“If the ones consuming my content were AI, I don’t know, but the viewers and audiences who consume it are still people,” Lee said.

	Archin Yen, director and VFX supervisor at WWWIND Studio, moderated the session. Asked how directors can keep AI from flattening their vision, Kim said AI tools can be learned in a few months, while film grammar such as the 180-degree rule, lenses and editing can take years. Most AI videos he sees default to eye-level, front-on bust shots that film and TV rarely use, he said.

	“Every VFX company in the world uses the same tools, but I think it differs depending on who uses them,” he said. “In the end, I think that human 5% decides the quality.”

title: ‘Pokemon’ Anime Studio OLM Trains AI Coloring Tool on Just Three Frames in Japan Government-Backed Project
description: OLM, the Japanese animation group behind the “Pokemon” anime series and films, has developed an AI coloring tool that picks up a show’s look from j
body:
OLM, the Japanese animation group behind the “Pokemon” anime series and films, has developed an AI coloring tool that picks up a show’s look from just three hand-painted frames, OLM Digital board director Yotsukura Tatsuo said at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.

	The tool came out of ANIMINS, a 15-month research project Yotsukura led under GENIAC, a generative AI program overseen by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. The project, which looked at how anime creators could put AI to use, wrapped in February.
	

	Because AI models usually need vast amounts of training data that studios struggle to assemble, OLM took the opposite approach. An artist colors three frames by hand, and the system learns that show’s line shapes and color palette on the spot in about 90 seconds, then colors each remaining frame in around 15 seconds. The more frames an artist paints by hand, the more accurate it becomes.

	“Strictly speaking, it isn’t generative AI,” Yotsukura said.

	Training only on a production’s own frames means no other works are harmed, he added, and the tool can adapt immediately when a new character or creature, such as a dragon, appears. The point OLM most wanted to stress, he said, is that it fits into existing anime workflows without disrupting them. At proof-of-concept stage, Yotsukura estimated it has cut painting workload by around 30%, though the checkers who review every colored frame have somewhat more to do.

	Toon Boom Animation, the Canadian maker of animation software Harmony and Storyboard Pro, is tackling the same bottleneck. Product marketing director Harry Ravelomanantsoa said the beta of the coloring tool in Ember, the company’s AI suite, is wrapping up, and in-betweening is expected to enter beta within a couple of weeks. One Manila studio that tested the coloring tool cut the painting time on a scene of 90 seconds to two minutes from 15 hours to two or three.
	

	OLM employs around 600 staff across Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and the U.S. “As you probably saw passing through the first floor, we make the ‘Pokemon’ anime – not the games – including the TV series and the theatrical films,” Yotsukura said, referring to the 2026-27 Pokemon Asia Championship Series: Taiwan Premier Ball League, held Nov. 7–8 on a lower floor of the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, where TCCF is running Nov. 6–9.

	The group’s slate also includes kids’ titles “Beyblade” and “Hanakappa” and the adult-skewing “The Apothecary Diaries.” Yotsukura, who also serves as CTO for the group’s Malaysian and Thai arms, noted that an in-house R&D division is unusual for a Japanese animation company.

	The group is experimenting with AI for in-betweening as well. But Yotsukura said the bigger gains may come from indirect uses across productions that involve more than 100 staff. With a startup partner from the GENIAC project, OLM is exploring anime-specific AI agents that could help new directors or production managers joining a series that has run for a decade or more, for instance by recalling what a director intended for a given cut. Agents could also speed up approvals and license management for secondary uses of its titles, which Yotsukura called the most revenue-critical part of the business. Because those areas are sensitive, OLM is proceeding with care, he said.

	Yotsukura likened the gap between AI demos and production reality to gacha, the Japanese capsule-toy machines where each JPY500 ($3.30) turn may or may not yield the prize you want – roughly what an AI generation credit costs, he said. AI gets close enough to 80% to raise expectations. “Raising it from there to 90 or 100% turns into work so hard it can make you heartsick.”

	Hobbyists may be happy with 80%, he said, but professional animators need tools that return their direction 100% of the time and let them make corrections. Anime is also highly sensitive to color, and AI tools that edit an image can shift its RGB values even when the result looks fine.

	“The creative stays with the artist, and the mechanical time goes to AI, to Ember,” Ravelomanantsoa said.

	Yotsukura said he agreed almost entirely with that split. “AI can only do what it has learned,” he said, adding that the kind of images that move audiences in cinemas, and the never-before-seen ideas behind hit anime, still have to come from people.
	

	He compared AI’s arrival to that of 3DCG, which took around 20 years to be accepted in anime. “Twenty years ago, I kept rejecting it, saying, ‘How could this ever be used in anime?’ Now it’s unthinkable for anime not to have 3DCG,” he said. AI will move far faster, Yotsukura said, because its quality is already high from the start.

	Charles Beirnaert, chief creative officer of Blue Spirit, the French studio behind Netflix’s “Blue Eye Samurai,” said the studio uses no AI at all on that series. “We’re not allowed to use AI for the Netflix projects,” he said. Blue Spirit asks every time at what stage AI might be permitted, he added, and the answer is always no – though he acknowledged the rule may not apply to every Netflix partner. On an Amazon series, the studio may use AI only to pre-visualize characters and robots, with none of it reaching the final image. Netflix’s published guidelines for production partners, issued in August 2025, require them to disclose any intended use of generative AI, with written approval needed for certain uses, including generative AI material in the final product.

	Away from those shows, Beirnaert’s team is testing AI on a series it is greenlighting as a conventional CG show, with a shorter YouTube version under consideration. A team of around 20 spent roughly three months on the traditional pilot. Using AI, one person recreated that work, covering everything from modeling and layout to animation, within days. The animation fell short of the original, Beirnaert said, but the backgrounds came out better.

	“For me, AI is not meant to replace animators. The day every animator is replaced, I will change job and do something else,” Beirnaert said.

	The two diverged when an audience member asked how much money AI could save. Beirnaert offered what he called a random estimate of €1 million on an €8 million budget, and said AI may help projects that stall at 80%–90% financed find the rest. Yotsukura said OLM is in a different position: it is brought in only after a budget is fixed, and sees AI as a way to gain more creative freedom within that budget rather than to shrink it. A year or two ago, the question was how many staff AI could replace, he said. Now it is shifting toward new shots that AI tools made possible.
	

	Moderator Kao Chieh, a lecturer at Shih Chien University, put the split down to a difference between Eastern and Western animation companies.

	Japanese anime already has creativity in abundance, Yotsukura said, but technology could play a bigger part, with the two driving the industry forward like a pair of wheels. “I think ‘not using AI’ is probably no longer an option from here on,” he said.

title: Papua New Guinea’s Most Expensive Film, ‘Mussau: The First Song,’ Wraps Shoot, Unveils First Looks (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Papua New Guinea’s most expensive film to date, the $4.5 million historical drama “Mussau: The First Song,” has wrapped principal photography after
body:
Papua New Guinea’s most expensive film to date, the $4.5 million historical drama “Mussau: The First Song,” has wrapped principal photography after a 40-day shoot across two provinces.

	Filming took place on Mussau Island in New Ireland Province and in Goroka, in Eastern Highlands Province. PNG-based producer NAFA Productions celebrated the wrap at a Thanksgiving event in Port Moresby on Saturday. Government figures at the event included Belden Norman Namah, Minister for Arts, Culture and Tourism; Chief Secretary Ivan Pomaleu; and Chief Censor Jim Abani.
	

	Indian director Bijukumar Damodaran, a three-time Indian National Film Award winner, is at the helm. Parul Agrawal produces, and Noelene Taula Wunum is executive producer.

	Inspired by a true story and set in the 1930s, the film centers on Taula Livovoa, a young islander who walks away from tribal violence and takes up a faith that is new to him. His choice sets off a sweeping social change that the producers rank among the South Pacific’s most remarkable.



	

					“Mussau: The First Song”
									NAFA Productions
	



	The dialogue is in six languages: Mussau, Emirau, Agarabi, Gadsup, Tok Pisin and English. Some of them are indigenous languages with small numbers of speakers that are at risk of dying out. The producers present the film as a way to protect the country’s linguistic and cultural heritage and bring it to a global audience.

	Much of the cast was drawn from the local community, and many are acting on screen for the first time. Some had never watched a film before. Several roles are played by great-grandchildren of the real people whose lives inspired the story. Two British actors round out the ensemble.
	

	Mussau Island has little infrastructure and patchy communications, which made the shoot hard to pull off. The 120-person crew, 20 of them technicians from India, spent 30 hours at sea crossing the Pacific to reach the island. Temporary lodging and facilities were set up there. Islanders helped throughout, including on sequences shot in the sea at high tide. The unit then moved on to Goroka to finish filming.

	“This has been one of the most challenging and rewarding journeys of my filmmaking career,” Damodaran said. “The people of Mussau welcomed us into their lives, their culture and their history, and their contribution has been invaluable. Having descendants of the original historical figures portray some of these characters, alongside community members who had never seen a film before, made this journey even more profound.”

	Hilda Tanimia wrote the story. The screenplay is by Jennifer Litau, who also served as translator, along with Joses Imona and Damodaran. The cinematographer is Yedhu Radhakrishnan and the editor is Davis Palakal Manuel. Arnold Laena handled production design and Gladice John designed the costumes. The music comes from Music Masters of PNG and the Murat Choir. The cast includes Freddy Sutchiff, Candy Ali, Daniel Lee Hird, Kevin Jackson, Jamie Napo, Calvin, Alan Balalua, Frank Eke and Dolvin Aite.



	

					“Mussau: The First Song”
									NAFA Productions
	



	NAFA Productions wants the film to bow at a top-tier international festival in 2027. It also hopes the film will be Papua New Guinea’s official entry for best international feature at the 100th Academy Awards.

	Damodaran has made that run once before. His earlier PNG–India co-production “Papa Buka” was the first film Papua New Guinea ever submitted to the Oscars’ international feature race.

schema.headline: Papua New Guinea’s Most Expensive Film, ‘Mussau: The First Song,’ Wraps Shoot, Unveils First Looks (EXCLUSIVE)

title: U2’s The Edge Wrote an ‘Elf’ Sequel, But It ‘Petered Out and Never Happened,’ Says Andy Richter
description:
According to Andy Richter, U2’s the Edge penned a script for a sequel to “Elf” — but fans will likely never get to see (or read) it.

	On a recent
body:
According to Andy Richter, U2’s the Edge penned a script for a sequel to “Elf” — but fans will likely never get to see (or read) it.

	On a recent episode of “Obsessed: The Podcast,” the actor explained that Shauna Robertson, who’d produced the original film, once received a message saying that the band member, also known as David Howell Evans, had written a script for “Elf 2”


	“Somebody reached out to her and said, ‘The Edge from U2 has written a sequel to ‘Elf,’ and he wants to talk to you about it,’” Richter said. “It’s the weirdest story, but apparently it was fully written. Somewhere in the world there is an Edge-penned ‘Elf 2’ out there… I would love for that to make the light of day. It never happened. It’s one of those things where she’s like, ‘All right, sure, I’ll meet him,’ and then it just petered out and never happened.”
	

	In addition to the Edge, “Old School” and “The Hangover Part II” writer Scot Armstrong penned a separate sequel script about “the evil South Pole elves kidnapping Santa or something like that,” said Richter. (He also noted that Armstrong had helped write “Elf,” but wasn’t credited for guild and procedural reasons.)

	And yet despite how beloved the holiday classic remains 23 years later, Richter is steadfast in the belief that a sequel isn’t necessary at this point. “I’m on the side of ‘Let it stand,’” he said. ”Just let ‘Elf’ be ‘Elf.’ You don’t have to use every part of the animal.”

	He continued: “Now that time has passed, the movie has become so special that I think that people, rightfully so, are loath to mess with it because we all can think of movies that have been tarnished by their sequels. And this is so special and so perfect and so beloved… Why risk it?”
	

	“Elf,” directed by Jon Favreau, originally hit theaters in 2003, starring Will Ferrell, James Caan, Zooey Deschanel, Mary Steenburgen and others. The Christmas classic followed Buddy the elf (Ferrell), who travels from the North Pole to New York City to meet his biological father, Walter Hobbs (Caan).

	Ritcher appeared briefly in the film as one of Hobbs’ colleagues and co-wrote the book “Elf Unwrapped: Behind the Scenes of a Modern Christmas Classic,” released Tuesday.

schema.headline: U2’s The Edge Wrote an ‘Elf’ Sequel, But It ‘Petered Out and Never Happened,’ Says Andy Richter

title: ‘Club Kid’ Scene-Stealer Kirby Howell-Baptiste on Playing a Drugged-Up Party Girl Who Turns Jordan Firstman’s World Upside Down: She’s ‘A Complete Tornado’
description:
“Should we do a bump?”

	It’s a line said, in various forms, numerous times across the first half of “Club Kid,” Jordan Firstman‘s hedonistic and h
body:
“Should we do a bump?”

	It’s a line said, in various forms, numerous times across the first half of “Club Kid,” Jordan Firstman‘s hedonistic and heartfelt coming-of-age comedy drama about a hard-partying New York club promoter suddenly forced to grapple with life and responsibilities. But the most hilariously-timed utterance comes in the middle of a crucial scene — one that shifts the entire movie — and from and by a minor, yet unforgettably wild, character.
	

	“She’s a massive party girl — she never sleeps, she only parties,” says Brit actor Kirby Howell-Baptiste of how Edison was described to her. “She’s completely lost all social boundaries. The lifetime of drugs melted half of her brain away, and all her social cues and etiquette have gone.”

	Howell-Baptiste’s etiquette-free Edison is only in “Club Kid” for a few minutes, but manages to steal the crucial scene in question from under the nose of writer, director and lead star Firstman.

	Roughly quarter of the way into the film, she rocks up unannounced and chaotic, sporting green braids and oversized sunglasses, at the apartment lived in by nightclub promoter Peter (Firstman), with 10-year-old Arlo (Reggie Absolom) in tow. While wandering around the place like it’s her own, she reveals — in a hysterically matter-of-fact manner — that not only is Arlo his, but she’s brought the kid across from the U.K. to live with him permanently. Boom.

	But Peter is gay — and confidently declares that he’s never slept with a woman. Not true, Edison asserts as she casually roams the kitchen on the hunt for literally anything remotely looking like drugs she can swallow or snort. He had sex with her friend Leonine a decade earlier at one of his nights while so high on ketamine, cocaine, GHB and (probably) more that he didn’t have a clue what was going on.
	

	“Nah, you fucked her, babes,” Edison says. “Point is, that’s your son.”

	Tragically, Leonine — as her apparent friend explains while sniffing some white powder she found on the counter — struggled with mental health issues (“She was in and out of the loony bin… what do you call it, rehab?”) and recently ended her life. “Last week she goes and tops herself — she fucking killed herself, babe.”

	In the midst of making these life-changing and upsetting revelations in the most wonderfully insensitive manner possible, Edison inquires if Peter and her should “do a bump” of coke (slightly shaken by how his life is quickly unravelling, he declines).

	“[Edison] is just a complete tornado,” says Londoner Howell-Baptiste, adding that she thinks the character is an “amalgamation of a few party people” Firstman has encountered. “But what I really love is that, although she’s absolutely bananas, she does feel quite real and quite relatable. I think everyone knows that person, to some degree. At some point in your life, you have met that person.” 

	Edison isn’t seen again in “Club Kid” after the apartment scene, in which she eventually leaves Arlo in Peter’s care and — predictably — fails to return to collect him as promised later on. But as Peter begins a frantic search to find her across various New York house parties, further levels of her comically debauched behaviour come to light, as he hears how she was kicked out of several places for simply being too much of a tornado to handle. 

	“I wasn’t part of those scenes, obviously, but what was really cool was that you got more of a picture of Edison,” she says. “Even in her absence, you got more of a picture of what she was doing and how she was just belligerently running around New York, hoovering up drugs at everyone’s party.”



	

					Kirby Howell-Baptiste as Edison in ‘Club Kid’
	



	Howell-Baptiste admits she had no idea who Firstman was when she was originally invited to audition for “Club Kid” in mid 2025. As someone who’s “not really on social media much” she missed his breakout during the COVID-19 pandemic. But she checked out some of his Instagram videos and thought he was funny. Crucially, the casting was being done by Carmen Cuba, who she says has “really exquisite taste” and thought, while she hadn’t seen the full script, the role seemed fun — “and the character was a party girl and I felt like I could channel that pretty well.” 
	

	A few months later, shooting in New York, Howell-Baptiste still didn’t have a full picture of what “Club Kid” was all about (she admits to only watching it in September), but her main takeaway was that Edison was written by someone “who knows how to party.”

	While the scene they shot was “almost verbatim” from the audition, there was a bit of ad-libbing, with Howell-Baptiste being the one who added the British slang term “tops herself.”

	“And afterwards, everyone was like, ‘What do you you mean ‘”tops herself”?’ Because, obviously, we’re in a film that’s written by a gay man. There’s so much about it that celebrates queer culture, and topping has a completely different meaning there,” she says. Despite offering to remove the word, she was told to keep it in. “It made the cut — and it think it’s really fun and adds even more confusion when it comes to American audiences being like: ‘What is going on with this girl?'”

	In terms of notes from Firstman, she says the main discussion was how he wanted Edison’s voice to sound, with the request that — alongside the British accent — she was “very hoarse, like she’s been up all night and almost always lost her voice.”

	To achieve this, Howell-Baptiste channelled former Spice Girl Mel B. “She always had this slight hoarseness singing that I always thought was very cool, so that’s where my mind went,” she says.

	Having shot her key scene (and the even shorter scene in which Edison and Leonine first meet Peter in the club) in the fall of 2025, Howell-Baptiste — whose long line of credits include “Killing Eve,” “Barry” and “Hacks” — moved on to other acting jobs. Several months later, while filming Season 3 of British TV drama “Sherwood,” Firstman messaged her to tell her that “Club Kid” had been accepted into Cannes. “I was like, ‘How incredible,’ but that was sort of it for me for a very long time.”

	Of course, “Club Kid” wound up being the talk of the festival festival, the breakout hit that sparked an intense bidding war eventually won by A24 for the princely sum of $17 million. Howell-Baptiste was oblivious to it all (“I joke that I live under a rock”) until her manager messaged her saying “Are you aware of everything that’s going on with ‘Club Kid’ in Cannes?” Keeping with the theme, it was a makeup artist who later informed her that “Club Kid” was going to Toronto. “I just wasn’t aware of any of the buzz!”
	

	Thankfully, Howell-Baptiste was able to attend the premiere at the BFI London Film Festival and took to the stage at the Royal Festival Hall with Firstman and Absolom, staying to watch the film to experience the laughs, cheers and tears from a hugely enthusiastic audience. Now, she can finally enjoy having a crucial — and spectacularly funny — role in one of the standout movies of the year.

	“I filmed in a complete vacuum — I just did one scene with three other characters and filmed the party scene, which was just one night,” she says. “So it’s all come as a really pleasant surprise to me — it’s lovely.”

schema.headline: ‘Club Kid’ Scene-Stealer Kirby Howell-Baptiste on Playing a Drugged-Up Party Girl Who Turns Jordan Firstman’s World Upside Down: She’s ‘A Complete Tornado’

title: French Cinema Is Thriving at Festivals but Facing an Uphill Battle in U.S. Theaters as Distributors Navigate a Shrinking Market
description: French cinema may be enjoying a golden run on the festival circuit and in the awards race, but getting those films into U.S. theaters, and persuadi
body:
French cinema may be enjoying a golden run on the festival circuit and in the awards race, but getting those films into U.S. theaters, and persuading American audiences to buy tickets, has become an increasingly uphill battle.

	That paradox was at the heart of a lively discussion at the American French Film Festival on Thursday, held in partnership with the CNC and Variety, where three veteran U.S. distributors painted a sobering picture of a market squeezed by shrinking theatrical opportunities.
	

	The panel brought together Robert Aronson, executive VP of Cohen Media Group; John Gerrans, co-president of Strand Releasing; and Paul Hudson, CEO of Outsider Pictures, who have collectively brought hundreds of international films to American audiences.

	The challenges extend well beyond French cinema. With fewer distributors acquiring independent films and arthouse theaters increasingly turning to mainstream Hollywood fare, even critically acclaimed movies are struggling to secure meaningful theatrical runs.

	The definition of a French-language box office hit has also changed dramatically along with the health of the special market for most foreign-language films. Jean-Pierre Jeunet’s cult film “Amélie” grossed approximately $33 million domestically a quarter-century ago. By comparison, Justine Triet’s Palme d’Or winner “Anatomy of a Fall,” one of the most successful French films of the last five years which was handled by Neon and won an Oscar, earned around $5 million in the U.S..

	The most accessible French blockbusters aren’t necessarily easier to market in the U.S. Samuel Goldwyn, whose company released Pathé’s two-part “The Three Musketeers” and “The Count of Monte Cristo,” and recently acquired Antonin Baudry’s historical epic saga “De Gaulle,” told Variety in a separate interview following the panel that these films have far broader commercial potential than their limited theatrical exposure suggests.
	

	“The only thing that makes it an arthouse movie is because it’s in a foreign language,” Goldwyn said of “De Gaulle,” adding that it could easily play on 1,000 screens if it were in English. He’s still managed to roll out the first opus of the WWII saga into theaters this weekend across key U.S. markets simultaneously with transactional VOD. 

	Yet while the pool of U.S. buyers has narrowed, competition remains fierce for the most coveted titles. Deep-pocketed players including Neon, Netflix, Mubi, A24 and Sony Pictures Classics continue to chase high-profile international films, particularly those from established auteurs. And even though Sony Pictures Classics, historically one of the most prolific U.S. buyers of French cinema, has become more selective, it’s still on the lookout for certain titles. The company just bought “Violette,” Jeunet’s latest film, and Louis Clichy’s animated feature “Iron Boy,” which won a prize at Cannes’ Un Certain Regard and was shortlisted as France’s Oscar submission alongside “De Gaulle.” The distributor also scored a solid theatrical run with Rebecca Zlotowski’s “A Private Life,” starring Jodie Foster, earlier this year.

	But for smaller distributors, competing for films with the greatest commercial potential is often a losing game.

	“We all see the same thing. So usually you go, boy, I could sell that. There’s something in here that I know I can sell. It’s got great reviews. It was in competition in Cannes or Berlin. And then Netflix buys it,” says Gerrans.

	In any case, securing screens can prove even harder than winning a bidding war. Arthouse theaters that once championed foreign-language cinema are increasingly booking Hollywood releases, while others have shuttered altogether.

	“We have to struggle to get into those theaters that used to be” devoted to arthouse films, Aronson said. Cohen Media Group owns the Landmark Theatres circuit, but that doesn’t guarantee bookings for its international releases. “They keep their own books and they have their own agenda and they need to be profitable,” said Aronson, whose recent acquisitions include László Nemes’ Cannes competition period drama “Moulin” and Géraldine Nakache’s “Think Good,” which played in Un Certain Regard.
	

	The company has also picked up Marc Fitoussi’s “All About Corinne,” starring Isabelle Huppert as a struggling film extra who dreams of becoming an actress and befriends a movie star played by Sandrine Kiberlain. Aronson, who compared the comedy’s tone to the French hit series “Call My Agent” (which was partly directed by Fitoussi), said star power remains a crucial selling point. 

	Strand has acquired Ulrike Ottinger’s experimental German-language vampire movie “The Blood Countess,” also starring Huppert, and Gerrans said her involvement has made a significant difference.

	“We’re able to book it because of her, and we’re getting a lot of festivals because of her,” Gerrans said. “So that one’s sort of booking itself, and that doesn’t happen too often.”

	For less recognizable titles, the outlook is considerably tougher. Gerrans admitted that he sometimes consults exhibitors before committing to acquisitions, particularly when sales agents require a theatrical release.

	“A lot of times we hold off and we ask some of the exhibitors, if I acquire this, will you play this film?” said Gerrans, whose upcoming French releases include “Flesh and Fuel” and “Daughters of Abraham.”

	He recalled pitching a film he loved to a New York exhibitor, only to be turned down. “It’s a fantastic film. You’ll love it. I think the audience will love it. They just go, that storyline seems a little too small.”

	Hudson, whose recent acquisitions include Cannes Un Certain Regard title “Congo Boy,” which earned Bradley Fiomona Dembeasset the best actor prize, described a similarly brutal scramble for screens.

	“We’re all trying to get the IFC Film Center or the Quad or the Angelika to book the film in New York, and there’s, I don’t know, 45 of us with all eight films trying to get them into these” theaters, Hudson joked.

	With major New York arthouse venues often booked months in advance, distributors sometimes resort to renting screens just to secure a theatrical launch.

	And competition isn’t coming only from Hollywood blockbusters. Repertory screenings, television series playing in multiplexes and special events are also taking up valuable screen space.

	“I understand arthouse theaters playing reissues,” Hudson said. “And young audiences rediscovering ‘Raise the Red Lantern.’ Amazing. But what about the new films? What about the new filmmakers? Where are the new ones going to get space to find room in the marketplace with all of this other stuff?”
	

	The squeeze extends beyond theaters. With DVD revenues largely gone, TV sales collapsing and streaming licenses losing value, independent distributors have fewer ways to recoup their investments.

	“We have a really hard time getting our films on the streaming platforms,” Aronson said. “Things have changed a lot in that market because they’re not that interested anymore in kind of single U.S.-only, after-theatrical streaming deals with independent distributors.”

	Hudson was particularly scathing about Amazon Prime’s declining royalty rates. “They were paying 10 cents per hour viewed, which is awful. But then they cut the rate down to 1 cent per hour viewed. Then they cut the rate down to half a cent per hour viewed.”

	He said he and other independent distributors have pulled titles from Amazon Prime and are looking to alternative outlets including Tubi, Roku, Pluto and YouTube.

	Strand operates its own subscription streaming channel through Amazon, but Gerrans said “they could decide tomorrow to turn it off.”

	With traditional distribution avenues under pressure, festivals are becoming an increasingly important way for films to reach audiences.

	“Film festivals are kind of like another tier of distribution, another level of distribution,” Aronson said. “It’s a way most independent films get seen by anyone.”

	Distributors are also looking to younger moviegoers, particularly through Letterboxd, which has built a passionate community of Gen Z cinephiles. But reaching that demographic without substantial marketing budgets remains a challenge.

	“Letterboxd is a real opportunity for us to find a younger audience,” Hudson said, describing how a friend’s son has helped him navigate the platform and build a community around his films.

	Yet enthusiasm for cinema doesn’t necessarily translate into ticket sales for contemporary French films.

	“I can’t even get my teenage kids to go see my movies,” Gerrans said, citing Strand’s release of Agathe Riedinger’s “Wild Diamond,” about a 17-year-old aspiring reality television star. Despite a premise seemingly tailored to younger audiences, the film failed to take off.

	Still, distributors are experimenting with ways to build word of mouth around films that might otherwise struggle to find an audience.
	

	Gerrans is optimistic about “Flesh and Fuel,” which he described as “the gay trucker movie you’ve never seen before,” betting that its uplifting ending will resonate with moviegoers.

	Hudson, meanwhile, plans an extended theatrical rollout for “Congo Boy,” stretching from Black History Month through Juneteenth, even if bookings remain scarce.

	“I can do five months because nobody’s clamoring for this movie to go onto a subscription service. But I may only get seven bookings.”

	French institutions including the CNC, Unifrance and Villa Albertine are also helping distributors promote French cinema through festivals, promotional events and talent travel.

	“All that helps to generate awareness,” Hudson said. “We have no support from the government. I mean, everything we do is from our own pockets. Film’s commerce here, it’s not culture.”

	The discussion was one of several panels bringing together French and American industry figures at the American French Film Festival, which is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year with a lineup of 60 films and series. The festival’s industry program also featured American filmmaker Randal Kleiser and French director Pierre Salvadori discussing artificial intelligence, as well as a panel moderated by Writers Guild of America West member Yvette Foy with French screenwriters Coralie Amedeo, Fanny Burdino, Abdel Raouf Dafri and Thomas Finkielkraut. The French delegation also included directors Baudry (“De Gaulle”), Laïla Marrakchi (“Strawberries”), Fitoussi (“All About Corinne”), Lukas Dhont (“Coward”) and actor-director Raphaël Quenard (“Le rêve américain”), among others.

schema.headline: French Cinema Is Thriving at Festivals but Facing an Uphill Battle in U.S. Theaters as Distributors Navigate a Shrinking Market

title: Dad Allegedly Left Sleeping Daughter Outside Target to Save Spot in Line for Pokémon Cards
description:
South Carolina Dad Arrested
                          Allegedly Left Daughter at Target to Save S
body:
South Carolina Dad Arrested
                          Allegedly Left Daughter at Target to Save Spot in Pokémon Card Line
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            One father proved that you really don't gotta catch 'em all ... after being accused of leaving his sleeping 6-year-old daughter outside a Target to stand in line for Pokémon cards.
      
    
            John-Michael Dooley was arrested on Nov. 6 ... after witnesses claimed he left his daughter outside the store with a pillow and blanket at 1 AM and didn't return for over an hour ... the Charlestown PD shared.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            After witnesses called the cops, Dooley eventually strolled up and was arrested around 2:30 AM ... this, according to CPD.
      

            Once placed in custody, police say that Dooley 'fessed up to leaving her behind to keep his place in line and returning home.
      
    
            Dooley has been charged with unlawful conduct toward a child and is being held at the Al Cannon Detention Center.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Thankfully enough, his kid was unharmed ... and placed into emergency protective custody with social services.
      
    
            With his bond being set at $40,000, he's set to appear in court on Dec. 18 ... according to court records.
